verses.zh: 我要为我所亲爱的唱歌，是我所爱者的歌，论他葡萄园的事：我所亲爱的有葡萄园在肥美的山冈上。
verses.en: I[NOTE:1] will sing to my love—a song to my lover about his vineyard.[NOTE:2] My love had a vineyardon a fertile hill.[NOTE:3]
notes: It is uncertain who is speaking here. Possibly the prophet, taking the role of best man, composes a love song for his friend on the occasion of his wedding. If so, יָדִיד (yadid) should be translated “my friend.” The present translation assumes that Israel is singing to the Lord. The word דוֹד (dod, “lover”) used in the second line is frequently used by the woman in the Song of Solomon to describe her lover.

Israel, viewing herself as the Lord’s lover, refers to herself as his vineyard. The metaphor has sexual connotations, for it pictures her capacity to satisfy his appetite and to produce children. See Song 8:12.

Heb “on a horn, a son of oil.” Apparently קֶרֶן (qeren, “horn”) here refers to the horn-shaped peak of a hill (BDB 902 s.v.) or to a mountain spur, i.e., a ridge that extends laterally from a mountain (HALOT 1145 s.v. קֶרֶן; H. Wildberger, Isaiah, 1:180). The expression “son of oil” pictures this hill as one capable of producing olive trees. Isaiah’s choice of קֶרֶן, a rare word for hill, may have been driven by paronomastic concerns, i.e., because קֶרֶן sounds like כֶּרֶם (kerem, “vineyard”).
verses.commentary:
5:1 "Let me sing" This introductory VERB (BDB 1010, KB 1479, Qal
COHORTATIVE) is also used in Isa. 26:1 and 42:10. The NOUN
also appears in Isa. 5:1. Often songs were used to mark events (cf. Exod. 15:1; Num. 21:17; Jdg. 5:1;
1 Sam. 18:6).

Here the song is used to draw the attention of the passers-by, so that they would
stop and listen. This implies it was sung in the market place.

▣ "well-beloved. . .beloved" These are two different Hebrew words. The first one (BDB 391) is
usually used in poetry of a family member. The second one (BDB 187) is used often in Song of Songs for the
lover. Here it refers to a special field for which the owner had special expectations. This would have
resonated well with Judah's agricultural society.

▣ "vineyard" The grapevine (or vineyard) is often a symbol of national Israel (i.e., Exod. 15:17;
Ps. 80:8; Jer. 2:21; 12:10) as were the olive tree and the dove. Judah was seen by the prophets as the only
true "people of God." In John 15:1 Jesus says "I am the true vine," not faithless Israel. See full note online at John 15:1.

This parable about a vineyard is related to Jesus' parable of the wicked tenant farmers (Matt. 21:33-46;
Mark 12:1-12; Luke 20:9-19). The fact it is repeated in all three Synoptic Gospels shows its importance.

The following parable in Matt. 22:1-22 continues the theme of Israel's rejection and Gentile inclusion
(also note John 10:16). I have become a Partial Preterist. I hope you will look at my commentaries on the Olivet
Discourse and the book of Revelation. I see YHWH divorcing faithless Israel and marrying the faithful believers in Jesus!

▣ "fertile hill" "Hill" is literally the word "horn" (BDB 901) used in the sense of an isolated
hill positioned just right to receive the sunlight and sloped just right for the rain to drain. The perfect
"hill," perfectly prepared to be planted with the "best" grapevines, for the best harvest!

The ADJECTIVE "fertile" is literally "son of oil" or "son of fat"
(BDB 1032), which is Hebrew imagery for fertility and abundance (cf. Isa. 28:1,4).

verses.zh: 他刨挖园子，捡去石头，栽种上等的葡萄树，在园中盖了一座楼，又凿出压酒池；指望结好葡萄，反倒结了野葡萄。
verses.en: He built a hedge around it,[NOTE:1] removed its stones,and planted a vine.He built a tower in the middle of itand constructed a winepress.He waited for it to produce edible grapes,but it produced sour ones instead.[NOTE:2]
notes: Or, “dug it up” (so NIV); KJV “fenced it.’ See HALOT 810 s.v. עזק.

Heb “wild grapes,” i.e., sour ones (also in v. 4).sn At this point the love song turns sour as the Lord himself breaks in and completes the story (see vv. 3-6). In the final line of v. 2 the love song presented to the Lord becomes a judgment speech by the Lord.
verses.commentary:
5:2 There is a play on the VERB "do" (BDB 793, KB 889) in Isa. 5:2-5, used
seven times. It is translated

- yield, Isa. 5:2 (twice)

- do, Isa. 5:4 (twice), what God will do for His vineyard

- yield, Isa. 5:4 (twice)

- do, Isa. 5:5, what God will do to His rebellious, ungrateful vineyard

▣ "He dug it all around, removed its stones" This first VERB (BDB 740,
KB 810, Piel IMPERFECT with waw) is found only here in the OT. The KJV has
"fenced." Although I do not believe this is an accurate translation of the Hebrew word, it does fit the context. When
stones were dug out of a rocky field in Palestine, they were usually stacked into a fence. Often the vineyards
were protected by a ditch (also possible meaning of first VERB, REB) with a stone hedge
(LXX, Vulgate). It is surely possible that Isaiah is describing terracing techniques. The stones
would be used to level parts of the field.

It is also possible that the stones were put in piles and used to keep the grape clusters off
the ground (James Freeman, Manners and Customs of the Bible, pp. 360-363).

▣ "the choicest vine" This refers to the bright red grapes known as "sorek" (BDB 977 I, cf. Jer. 2:21).
These grapes got their name from a valley in Palestine (cf. Jdg. 16:4). They are mentioned in Jer. 2:21 as
being the most expensive and sought after variety of grapes. See UBS Fauna and Flora of the Bible, p. 190.

This grapevine species is even mentioned in a Messianic passage (cf. Gen. 49:11).

▣ "tower" This (BDB 153, "watchtower" built from stones dug out of the field) was
for security purposes and was usually occupied only during the planting time and the harvest time in
September (it would serve the same purpose as the word "booth" mentioned in Isa. 1:8). This same word
can refer to a military tower (cf. Isa. 2:15). Context, context, context!

▣ "hewed out a wine vat" This would have been a shallow man-made depression in a rock
surface which allowed the women to crush the grapes with their feet and then a channel in the rock to a
deeper depression where the juice would be stored.

▣ "Then He expected it to produce good grapes" YHWH did everything possible
(i.e. Rom. 9:4-5) to assure that His covenant people reflected His character to the nations, but they did not
(i.e. Ezek. 36:22-32). YHWH wanted all humans made in His image and likeness (i.e. Gen. 1:26-27) to know Him.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KNOW

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

NASB
"worthless one"

NKJV, NRSV, NJB, REB, JPSOA, Peshitta
"wild grapes"

TEV, JB
"every grape was sour"

LXX
"thorns"

The Hebrew term (BDB 93) can refer to

- stinking or noxious weeds, SINGULAR, cf. Job 31:40

- stinking things, worthless things, PLURAL

The basic root refers to the stink of

- corpses, Isa. 34:3 (cf. Isa. 5:25); Joel 2:20; Amos 4:10

- locusts, Joel 2:20 (imagery for a dead army)

The MT in this context refers to "wild grapes," which were not sweet and plump, but small
and sour, unfit to make wine.

verses.zh: 耶路撒冷的居民和犹大人哪，请你们现今在我与我的葡萄园中，断定是非。
verses.en: So now, residents of Jerusalem,[NOTE:1] people[NOTE:2] of Judah,you decide between me and my vineyard!
notes: For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.
Heb “men,” but in a generic sense.
verses.commentary:
5:3 The prophet is bringing his audience into a decision-making process. This is the point of the genre
of parable (see SPECIAL TOPIC: INTERPRETING PARABLES).
They will judge themselves!

The VERB "judge" (BDB 1047, KB 1622) is a Qal
IMPERATIVE and is similar to Matt. 21:40, which is Jesus' strongest condemnation of faithless Israel!

verses.zh: 我为我葡萄园所做之外，还有甚么可做的呢？我指望结好葡萄，怎么倒结了野葡萄呢？
verses.en: What more can I do for my vineyardbeyond what I have already done?When I waited for it to produce edible grapes,why did it produce sour ones instead?
verses.commentary:
5:4 This question is the heart of the love song. YHWH did everything for His people, but they
rejected Him (cf. Matt. 21:33-45; 22:14).

verses.zh: 现在我告诉你们，我要向我葡萄园怎样行：我必撤去篱笆，使它被吞灭，拆毁墙垣，使它被践踏。
verses.en: Now I will inform youwhat I am about to do to my vineyard:I will remove its hedge and turn it into pasture,[NOTE:1] I will break its wall and allow animals to graze there.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “and it will become [a place for] grazing.” בָּעַר (baʿar, “grazing”) is a homonym of the more often used verb “to burn.”
Heb “and it will become a trampled place” (NASB “trampled ground”).
verses.commentary:
5:5-6 The prophet, speaking for YHWH, declares (BDB 393, KB 390, Hiphil
COHORTATIVE) what He will do to His disappointing vineyard (i.e. His covenant people).

- remove its hedge, consequently it will be consumed by animals

- break down it's protective wall, consequently the vines will be trampled to the ground

- refuse to tend it, consequently the briars and thorns will come up (cf. Isa. 7:23,25; 9:18; 27:4)

- refuse to send rain, consequently it will dry up and die (cf. Deut. 28:23-24)

verses.zh: 我必使它荒废，不再修理，不再锄刨，荆棘蒺藜倒要生长。我也必命云不降雨在其上。
verses.en: I will make it a wasteland;no one will prune its vines or hoe its ground,[NOTE:1] and thorns and briers will grow there.I will order the cloudsnot to drop any rain on it.
notes: Heb “it will not be pruned or hoed” (so NASB); ASV and NRSV both similar.
verses.commentary:
5:6 "I will lay it waste" The VERB (BDB 1011, KB 1483) is a Qal
IMPERFECT. YHWH will make His vineyard a "waste" (BDB 144). The term is found
only here. It can mean "end" or "destruction." The judgment of YHWH is total and final (cf. Isa. 5:30)! Thank
God for chapters 7-12! There will be a new day (chapters 40-55) and a new heaven and earth (chapters 56-66, cf. Rev. 21-22).

▣ "I will also charge the clouds to rain no rain on it" Nature has been, and continues to be, affected
by mankind's sin (cf. Gen. 3:17-19 and Rom. 8:19-26). It is used by God for blessing or judgment (i.e., Lev. 26:4;
Deut. 11:14; 28:12; Amos 4:7; Zech. 14:17).

SPECIAL TOPIC: WATERS

verses.zh: 万军之耶和华的葡萄园就是以色列家；他所喜爱的树就是犹大人。他指望的是公平，谁知倒有暴虐（或译：倒流人血）；指望的是公义，谁知倒有冤声。
verses.en: Indeed,[NOTE:1] Israel[NOTE:2] is the vineyard of the Lord of Heaven’s Armies,the people[NOTE:3] of Judah are the cultivated place in which he took delight.He waited for justice, but look what he got—disobedience![NOTE:4] He waited for fairness, but look what he got—cries for help![NOTE:5]
notes: Or “For” (KJV, ASV, NASB, NRSV).
Heb “the house of Israel” (so NASB, NIV84, NRSV). NIV11 translates “the nation of Israel.”
Heb “men,” but in a generic sense.

Heb “but, look, disobedience.” The precise meaning of מִשְׂפָּח (mispakh), which occurs only here in the OT, is uncertain. Some have suggested a meaning “bloodshed.” The term is obviously chosen for its wordplay value; it sounds very much like מִשְׁפָּט (mishpat, “justice”). The sound play draws attention to the point being made; the people have not met the Lord’s expectations.

Heb “but, look, a cry for help.” The verb (“he waited”) does double duty in the parallelism. צְעָקָה (tseaʿqah) refers to the cries for help made by the oppressed. It sounds very much like צְדָקָה (tsedaqah, “fairness”). The sound play draws attention to the point being made; the people have not met the Lord’s expectations.
verses.commentary:
5:7 "the Lord of hosts" See SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord of Hosts

▣ "the house of Israel" This term normally seems to refer to all of Israel collectively
before the political split in 922 B.C., although in this verse the term refers
to Judah (line 2). At this time in the history of the people of God, their nation was split into the northern ten
tribes known as Israel, Ephraim, or Samaria and the southern three tribes known as Judah, which included
Judah, Benjamin, Simeon, and most of the Levites/priests.

▣ "justice. . .bloodshed. . .righteousness. . .a cry of distress" This is a play on two different
sounds in Hebrew that cannot be reproduced in an English translation:

- םשפט Mishpat (justice, BDB 1048)
vs. משׁפח Mispach (bloodshed,
BDB 705)

- צדק Zedakah (righteousness, BDB 842)
vs. צעק Zeakah (cry of distress, BDB 858)

Another biblical reversal of expectations.

verses.zh: 祸哉！那些以房接房，以地连地，以致不留余地的，只顾自己独居境内。
verses.en: Beware, those who accumulate houses,[NOTE:1] who also accumulate field after field[NOTE:2] until there is no land left,[NOTE:3] and you are the only landowners remaining within the land.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “Woe [to] those who make a house touch a house.”

Heb “[who] bring a field near a field.”sn This verse does not condemn real estate endeavors per se, but refers to the way in which the rich bureaucrats of Judah accumulated property by exploiting the poor, in violation of the covenantal principle that the land belonged to God and that every family was to have its own portion of land. See the note at 1:23.
Heb “until the end of the place”; NASB “until there is no more room.”
Heb “and you are made to dwell alone in the midst of the land.”
verses.commentary:
5:8

NASB, NKJV, NJB, REB, Pehsitta
"Woe"

NRSV, JPSOA, LXX
"Ah"

TEV
"You are doomed"

There is some debate among commentators as to whether there are six or seven "woes"
(BDB 222) listed. This is not literally the Hebrew term "woe" (BDB 17, which denotes a lament, cf.
Isa. 3:9,11; 6:5; 24:16). This translation suggestion from BDB is "ah," "alas," or "ha" (cf. Isa. 1:4;
10:1,5; 17:12; 28:1). It expresses painful dissatisfaction with the current situation or consequences.

They begin the consequences of judgment on Judah because of their straying from
YHWH's covenant. They are basically a listing of the sins of the Judean society.

▣ "to those who add house to house and join field to field" This refers to the greedy
land owners who exploited the poor by taking their ancestral lands (i.e., the land division by Joshua, cf.
Joshua 13-19) to accumulate more and more land for themselves (cf. Jer. 22:13-17; Micah 2:2). The law of Moses
protected the allotted lands by enacting "the Year of Jubliee" (cf. Lev. 25:8-55; Num. 36:4). All land must return
to the original tribal family owners every fiftieth year. Although there is no record in the OT of Israel ever
honoring this release, it was still the expressed will of God.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FEASTS OF ISRAEL, II. C.

verses.zh: 我耳闻万军之耶和华说：必有许多又大又美的房屋成为荒凉，无人居住。
verses.en: The Lord of Heaven’s Armies told me this:[NOTE:1] “Many houses will certainly become desolate,large, impressive houses will have no one living in them.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “in my ears, the Lord of armies [traditionally, the Lord of hosts].”
Heb “great and good [houses], without a resident.”
verses.commentary:
5:9 The opening of Isa. 5:9 is very emphatic, with no VERB, literally "in
my ears, the Lord of hosts." This is a clear claim of verbal divine revelation
(cf. Isa. 22:14)! This is not Isaiah's message, nor Isaiah's emotion! YHWH is shouting through His prophet
to His wayward people.

This judgment is similar to Amos 5:11 and Micah 6:15. The expectations of the rich and
exploitive elements of society will not materialize. They will not enjoy their ill-gotten gain! We reap
what we sow (see note at Isa. 3:10-11).

SPECIAL TOPIC: WAYS OF REVELATION

verses.zh: 三十亩葡萄园只出一罢特酒；一贺梅珥谷种只结一伊法粮食。
verses.en: Indeed, a large vineyard[NOTE:1] will produce just a few gallons,[NOTE:2] and enough seed to yield several bushels[NOTE:3] will produce less than a bushel.”[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “a ten-yoke vineyard.” The Hebrew term צֶמֶד (tsemed, “yoke”) is here a unit of square measure. Apparently a ten-yoke vineyard covered the same amount of land it would take ten teams of oxen to plow in a certain period of time. The exact size is unknown.
Heb “one bath.” A bath was a liquid measure. Estimates of its modern equivalent range from approximately six to twelve gallons.
Heb “a homer.” A homer was a dry measure, the exact size of which is debated. Cf. NCV “ten bushels”; CEV “five bushels.”
Heb “an ephah.” An ephah was a dry measure; there were ten ephahs in a homer. So this verse envisions major crop failure, where only one-tenth of the anticipated harvest is realized.
verses.commentary:
5:10 "For ten acres of vineyard" "Acres" is literally "a couple" or "a pair" (BDB 855, cf. 1 Sam. 14:14),
which denoted animals yoked together for agricultural purposes. One "yoke" was the amount of land an oxen could
plow in one day.

▣ "will yield only one bath of wine" The term "bath" (BDB 144 II) is a liquid
measurement in Hebrew and it is equal to eight to ten gallons (see

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANE WEIGHTS AND VOLUMES (Metrology). In this context it is imagery for the
fruitlessness of the usurped land.

▣ "And a homer of seed will yield but an ephah of grain" Again this is striking imagery
for the fruitlessness of the usurped land. We learn from Ezek. 45:11 that there were ten ephahs in one homer;
therefore, this is stating that if a farmer plants one hundred pounds, he will only harvest ten.

verses.zh: 祸哉！那些清早起来追求浓酒，留连到夜深，甚至因酒发烧的人。
verses.en: Beware, those who get up early to drink beer,[NOTE:1] those who keep drinking long after darkuntil they are intoxicated with wine.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “Woe [to] those who arise early in the morning, [who] chase beer.”

This verse does not condemn drinking per se, but refers to the carousing lifestyle of the rich bureaucrats, made possible by wealth taken from the poor. Their carousing is not the fundamental problem, but a disgusting symptom of the real disease—their social injustice.tn Heb “[who] delay until dark, [until] wine enflames them.”
verses.commentary:
5:11 "Woe to those who rise early in the morning that they may pursue strong drink" The next sin
mentioned is one of riotous pleasure-seeking from morning to evening. It needs to be stressed that the
Bible does not condemn wine, but it does condemn the abuse of wine. This same imagery of strong
drink is used in Isaiah 28. Other poignant passages on this subject are found in Prov. 20:1 and 23:29-35.
However, one must add the balance of Ps. 104:14-15; Eccl. 9:7.

"Strong drink" (BDB 1016) is a Hebrew term describing the addition of
intoxicating grain liquors to wine.

SPECIAL TOPIC: BIBLICAL ATTITUDES TOWARD ALCOHOL AND ALCOHOLISM

verses.zh: 他们在筵席上弹琴，鼓瑟，击鼓，吹笛，饮酒，却不顾念耶和华的作为，也不留心他手所做的。
verses.en: They have stringed instruments,[NOTE:1] tambourines, flutes,and wine at their parties.So they do not recognize what the Lord is doing,they do not perceive what he is bringing about.[NOTE:2]
notes: Two types of stringed instruments are specifically mentioned in the Hebrew text, the כִּנּוֹר (kinnor, “zither”) and נֶבֶל (nevel, “harp”).

Heb “the work of the Lord they do not look at, and the work of his hands they do not see.” God’s “work” can sometimes be his creative deeds, but in this context it is the judgment that he is planning to bring upon his people (cf. vv. 19, 26; 10:12; 28:21).
verses.commentary:
5:12 "Their banquets are accompanied by" This is a way of speaking of the cultural entertainment
of the day. It depicts a wealthy class given to worldly pleasures.

▣ "But they do not pay attention to the deeds of the Lord,

Nor do they consider the work of His hands" YHWH's covenant people's refusal to hear and
understand His will is a recurrent theme (cf. Isa. 1:2-3,10a; 5:12,13,24; 6:9-10; 30:9). YHWH had given them
spiritual ears and eyes (cf. Deut. 29:4), but their collective blindness and deafness had caused YHWH to remove the
possibility of comprehension (cf. Isa. 6:9-10; 29:9-10).

The tragedy of these verses is that the Judeans of Isaiah's day were depending on their own
resources and schemes instead of the provision of their Covenant God. One should compare Isa. 5:24d,e with
Deut. 8:11-20.

verses.zh: 所以，我的百姓因无知就被掳去；他们的尊贵人甚是饥饿，群众极其干渴。
verses.en: Therefore my[NOTE:1] people will be deported[NOTE:2] because of their lack of understanding.Their[NOTE:3] leaders will have nothing to eat,[NOTE:4] their[NOTE:5] masses will have nothing to drink.[NOTE:6]
notes: It is not certain if the prophet or the Lord is speaking at this point.
The suffixed (perfect) form of the verb is used; in this way the coming event is described for rhetorical effect as occurring or as already completed.
The third masculine singular suffix refers back to “my people.”

Heb “Their glory will be men of hunger.” כָּבוֹד (kavod, “glory”) is in opposition to הָמוֹן (hamon, “masses”) and refers here to the rich and prominent members of the nation. Some prefer to repoint מְתֵי (metey, “men of”) as מֵתֵי (metey, “dead ones of”).
The third masculine singular suffix refers back to “my people.”
Heb “and their masses will be parched [by] thirst.”
verses.commentary:
5:13-17 Here is a list of what will happen to Judah's wealthy, exploitive citizens.

- exiled, Isa. 5:13

- famished, Isa. 5:13

- parched, Isa. 5:13

- swallowed by Sheol, Isa. 5:14

- humbled, Isa. 5:15

- abused, Isa. 5:15 (twice)

- strangers eat of the fat of the wealthy, Isa. 5:17

5:13 "Therefore My people go into exile for their lack of knowledge" This is obviously a prediction
of exile. There has been some speculation about whether it refers to the Assyrian exiles (722 B.C.)
of the northern ten tribes or the Babylonian exiles of Judah (i.e., 605, 597, 586, 582 B.C.) of
the southern three tribes (plus most Levites). The immediate context seems to lend itself to either (this is
so common in Isaiah, maybe purposeful). Assyria is mentioned specifically in Isa. 7:18 and 10:5ff. I think that
Isa. 13:1-14:27 also refers to Assyria who destroyed the city of Babylon and Assyria's king took the title,
"King of Babylon."

The mention of an exile out of the Promised Land was shocking. Canaan was promised to
Abraham's seed (i.e. Genesis 12; 15). Now the covenant with the Patriarchs was being rescinded because of
Judah's disobedience to the covenant requirements (i.e. a conditional covenant). They rejoiced in and clung to
the promises, but ignored the requirements (cf. Jeremiah 7).

In a theological sense this parallels Genesis 2 (God's ideal fellowship with mankind) and
Genesis 3 (Adam and Eve's open-eyed rebellion). Mankind was driven out of the Garden of Eden (cf. Gen. 3:24).
This was unexpected and shocking! So too, the revelation of an exile. What was thought to be a permanent promise
by God was affected by human sin. In a similar way "the New Covenant" of Jer. 31:31-34 was a shocking revelation.
The everlasting covenants were being superceded because of human inability to perform their part of the covenant.
Therefore, a new relationship with God would need to be established based on

- God's performance (new heart, new mind, cf. Ezek. 36:22-36)

- mankind's enabling by God's Spirit to be obedient

God still wants a righteous people to reflect His character to a lost and needy world (i.e.,
the nations). The means of that "righteousness" have changed. Human ability proved to be inadequate (cf.
Galatians 3). The OT was a means of showing mankind's inability!

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS

SPECIAL TOPIC: EDEN

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND

▣ "for their lack of knowledge" This is a willful rejection of knowledge, not ignorance (cf.
Isa. 1:3; Hosea 4:6,14). Judah rebelled against the revealed will of YHWH (i.e., the Mosaic Covenant). She
left the clearly marked path!

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PATH, THE WAY

verses.zh: 故此，阴间扩张其欲，开了无限量的口；他们的荣耀、群众、繁华，并快乐的人都落在其中。
verses.en: So Death[NOTE:1] will open up its throat,and open wide its mouth;[NOTE:2] Zion’s dignitaries and masses will descend into it,including those who revel and celebrate within her.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “Sheol” (so ASV, NASB, NRSV); the underworld, the land of the dead, according to the OT world view. Cf. NAB “the nether world”; TEV, CEV “the world of the dead”; NLT “the grave.”

Heb “so Sheol will make wide its throat, and open its mouth without limit.”sn Death is portrayed in both the OT (Prov 1:12; Hab 2:5) and Canaanite myth as voraciously swallowing up its prey. In the myths Death is portrayed as having “a lip to the earth, a lip to the heavens…and a tongue to the stars.” (G. R. Driver, Canaanite Myths and Legends, 69, text 5 ii 2-3.) Death describes his own appetite as follows: “But my appetite is the appetite of lions in the waste….If it is in very truth my desire to consume ‘clay’ [a reference to his human victims], then in truth by the handfuls I must eat it, whether my seven portions [indicating fullness and completeness] are already in the bowl or whether Nahar [the god of the river responsible for ferrying victims from the land of the living to the land of the dead] has to mix the cup.” (Driver, 68-69, text 5 i 14-22).

Heb “and her splendor and her masses will go down, and her tumult and the one who exults in her.” The antecedent of the four feminine singular pronominal suffixes used in v. 14b is unclear. The likely referent is personified Zion/Jerusalem (see 3:25-26; 4:4-5).
verses.commentary:
5:14 "Sheol has enlarged its throat and opened its mouth without measure" "Sheol" is a Hebrew term (BDB 982)
which refers to"the realm of the dead." Here it is personified as an animal with a ravenous appetite
(cf. Prov. 1:12; 27:20; Hab. 2:5).

SPECIAL TOPIC: WHERE ARE THE DEAD?, I. B.

▣ "And Jerusalem's splendor, her multitude, her din of revelry, and the jubilant within her,
descent into it" This shows a total reversal of expectations!

verses.zh: 卑贱人被压服；尊贵人降为卑；眼目高傲的人也降为卑。
verses.en: Men will be humiliated,they will be brought low;the proud will be brought low.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “men are brought down, men are brought low, the eyes of pride are brought low.”
verses.commentary:
5:15 "So the common man will be humbled, and the man of importance abased" This is referring
to judgment on an entire society (cf. Isa. 2:9,12,17). There seems to be a theological contrast between the
Hebrew terms for "man," "adam" (BDB 9, NASB, "common man") and "Ish" (BDB 35, NASB,
"man of importance"). This same distinction can be seen in Isa. 2:9; 31:8.

▣ "The eyes of the proud will also be abased" This is a recurrent theme throughout Scripture and
is repeated in a slightly different way in Isa. 5:20 and 21 through the imagery of light and darkness.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LIFTED UP

verses.zh: 惟有万军之耶和华因公平而崇高；圣者　神因公义显为圣。
verses.en: The Lord of Heaven’s Armies will be exalted[NOTE:1] when he punishes,[NOTE:2] the holy God’s authority will be recognized when he judges.[NOTE:3]
notes: Or “elevated”; TEV “the Lord Almighty shows his greatness.”
Heb “by judgment/justice.” When God justly punishes the evildoers denounced in the preceding verses, he will be recognized as a mighty warrior.

The appearance of מִשְׁפָט (mishpat, “justice”) and צְדָקָה (tsedaqah, “fairness”) here is rhetorically significant, when one recalls v. 7. There God denounces his people for failing to produce a society where “justice” and “fairness” are valued and maintained. God will judge his people for their failure, taking “justice” and “fairness” into his own hands.tn Heb “The holy God will be set apart by fairness.” In this context God’s holiness is his sovereign royal authority, which implies a commitment to justice (see the note on the phrase “the sovereign king of Israel” in 1:4). When God judges evildoers as they deserve, his sovereignty will be acknowledged.
verses.commentary:
5:16 "But the Lord of hosts will be exalted in judgment" The descendants of
Abraham were chosen to reveal YHWH. They were to reveal Him in their faithfulness resulting in a stable and
abundant society or they will reveal Him in their waywardness resulting in His judgment.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣ "the holy God will show Himself holy in righteousness" This line of poetry is in a synonymous parallel
relationship to the previous line of poetry. Hebrew poetry must be interpreted in light of its paralellism!

SPECIAL TOPIC: HOLY

SPECIAL TOPIC: RIGHTEOUSNESS

verses.zh: 那时，羊羔必来吃草，如同在自己的草场；丰肥人的荒场被游行的人吃尽。
verses.en: Lambs[NOTE:1] will graze as if in their pastures,amid the ruins the rich sojourners will graze.[NOTE:2]
notes: Or “young rams”; NIV, NCV “sheep”; NLT “flocks.”

The image completes the picture begun in v. 14 and adds to the irony. When judgment comes, Sheol will eat up the sinners who frequent the feasts; then the banqueting halls will lie in ruins and only sheep will eat there.tc The Hebrew text reads literally, “and ruins, fatlings, resident foreigners, will eat.” This part of the verse has occasioned various suggestions of emendation. The parallelism is tighter if the second line refers to animals grazing. The translation, “amid the ruins the fatlings and young sheep graze,” assumes an emendation of “resident foreigners” (גָּרִים, garim) to “young goats/sheep” (גְּדַיִם, gedaim)—confusion of dalet and resh is quite common—and understands “fatlings” and “young sheep” as a compound subject or as in apposition as the subject of the verb. However, no emendations are necessary if the above translation is correct. The meaning of מֵחִים (mekhim) has a significant impact on one’s textual decision and translation. The noun can refer to a sacrificial (“fat”) animal as it does in its only other occurrence (Ps 66:15). However, it could signify the rich of the earth (cf. Ps 22:29 [MT 30]: “the fat ones of the earth”), using a different word for “fatness” (Ps 22:29: דָּשֶׁן, dashen). If so, it serves a figurative reference to the rich. Consequently, the above translation coheres with the first half of the verse. Just as the sheep are out of place grazing in these places (“as in their pasture”), the sojourners would not have expected to have the chance to eat in these locations. Both animals and itinerant foreigners would eat in places not normal for them.
verses.commentary:
5:17 "Then the lambs will graze as in their pasture,

And strangers will eat in the waste places of the wealthy" There has been much
discussion among commentators about the exact relationship of this verse to the preceding context. Some say

- it refers to God's care for those remaining in the land

- it refers to God's judgment of the wealthy landowners

- it refers to the remaining Jewish remnant after the exile

- it refers to Gentiles resettled in Judah's territory after the exile of her citizens

It seems to me that the immediate context of judgment must relate it to the destruction and
judgment of the wealthy and the ruin of their illegally procured land. It is public land now!

The JPSOA footnote suggests an emendation based on Ezek. 34:17-22, where a
distinction is made between:

- lambs vs. rams/male goats

- lean sheep vs. fat sheep

This would continue Isaiah 5's condemnation of the rich and powerful exploiters of His faithful
poor and powerless followers.

The UBS Text Project, pp. 12-13, gives three ways to interpret these lines of poetry. If
this is a crucial issue for you, see that detailed textual study.

SPECIAL TOPIC: WEALTH

verses.zh: 祸哉！那些以虚假之细绳牵罪孽的人！他们又像以套绳拉罪恶，
verses.en: Beware, those who pull evil along using cords of emptiness are as good as dead,[NOTE:1] who pull sin as with cart ropes.[NOTE:2]
notes: See the note at v. 8.

The Hebrew text reads literally, “Woe to those who pull evil with the ropes of emptiness, and, as [with] ropes of a cart, sin.” Though several textual details are unclear, the basic idea is apparent. The sinners are so attached to their sinful ways (compared here to a heavy load) that they strain to drag them along behind them. If שָׁוְא (shaveʾ, “emptiness”) is retained, it makes a further comment on their lifestyle, denouncing it as one that is devoid of what is right and destined to lead to nothing but destruction. Because “emptiness” does not form a very tight parallel with “cart” in the next line, some emend שָׁוְא to שֶׂה (se, “sheep”) and עֲגָלָה (ʿagalah, “cart”) to עֵגֶל (ʿegel, “calf”): “Those who pull evil along with a sheep halter are as good as dead, who pull sin with a calf rope” (following the lead of the LXX and improving the internal parallelism of the verse). In this case, the verse pictures the sinners pulling sin along behind them as one pulls an animal with a halter. For a discussion of this view, see J. N. Oswalt, Isaiah (NICOT), 1:163, n. 1. Nevertheless, this emendation is unnecessary. The above translation emphasizes the folly of the Israelites who hold on to their sin (and its punishment) even while they hope for divine intervention.
verses.commentary:
5:18-23 Another strophe of "woes" on the wicked is enumerated because

- Isa. 5:18, they lead evil around like an animal on a leash

- Isa. 5:19, they demand YHWH to quickly fulfill His covenant promises (without regard for the covenant
requirements)

- Isa. 5:20, this may be related to Isa. 5:19. When God does not act the way they wanted, they called
His acts evil, dark, and bitter

- Isa. 5:21, they assume their own wisdom to be true and God's false (Isa. 5:19-20)

- Isa. 5:22, they are drunkards

- Isa. 5:23, they use bribery to achieve their ends

These are manipulative religious egotists!

5:18-19 "Woe to those who drag iniquity with the cords of falsehood,

And sin as if with cart ropes" The Hebrew is uncertain. This seems to refer
to a group of people whom I have designated as practical atheists. They admit YHWH's existence theologically, but
refuse to walk in this knowledge. They choose to live as if there were no God and even taunt His
existence (cf. Isa. 5:19). They hold on to their sin at any cost! They are tied/bound to their
self-centered lifestyles!

5:18 "Woe" See note at 1:8.

▣

NASB, NKJV, NRSV, NJB, JPSOA
"as if with cart ropes"

Peshitta
"a bridle on the neck of a heifer"

LXX
"as with a strap from a

heifer's yoke"

REB
"a heifer's rope"

The MT has "of the cart" (BDB 722), but the word for "heifer" is spelled exactly
the same but with different vowel points.

- העגלה ‒ the cart

- העגלה ‒ the heifer

The UBS Text Project, p. 13, gives "of the cart" a "B" rating (some doubt). Both fit
the poetic parallelism.

verses.zh: 说：任他急速行，赶快成就他的作为，使我们看看；任以色列圣者所谋划的临近成就，使我们知道。
verses.en: They say, “Let him hurry, let him act quickly,[NOTE:1] so we can see;let the plan of the Holy One of Israel[NOTE:2] take shape[NOTE:3] and come to pass,then we will know it!”
notes: Heb “let his work hurry, let it hasten.” The pronoun “his” refers to God, as the parallel line makes clear. The reference to his “work” alludes back to v. 12, which refers to his “work” of judgment. With these words the people challenged the prophet’s warning of approaching judgment. They were in essence saying that they saw no evidence that God was about to work in such a way.
See the note on the phrase “the Holy One of Israel” in 1:4.
Heb “draw near” (so NASB); NRSV “hasten to fulfillment.”
verses.commentary:
5:19 There are several commands in this verse.

- let Him make speed, BDB 554, KB 553, Piel IMPERFECT used
in a JUSSIVE sense

- let Him hasten, BDB 301, KB 300, Hiphil COHORTATIVE

- let the purpose of the Holy One of Israel draw near, BDB 897, KB 1132, Qal
IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense

- come to pass, BDB 97, KB 112, Qal COHORTATIVE

- that we may know it, BDB 393, KB 390, Qal COHORTATIVE

To whom does verse 19 refer?

- It relates to those wealthy faithless Judeans who do not pay attention to YHWH's revelation (cf. 5:12).

- It relates to faithful Israelites who want YHWH to act quickly on their behalf (The Jewish Study Bible, p. 794).

The context of v. 18 favors option #1.

The NASB Study Bible makes an interesting comment about #1 and #2 above.

"The Hebrew for the words 'make speed' and 'hasten' correspond to that of the first and
third elements of the name 'Maher-shalal-hash-baz' (meaning 'swift is the booty, speedy is the prey,'
see Isa. 8:1,3), he may have been responding to the sarcastic taunts of sinners" (p. 967).

▣ "the Holy One of Israel" "The Holy One of Israel" is a title for Deity so common in Isaiah; see note
at Isa. 1:4; and SPECIAL TOPIC: THE HOLY ONE)

verses.zh: 祸哉！那些称恶为善，称善为恶，以暗为光，以光为暗，以苦为甜，以甜为苦的人。
verses.en: Beware, those who call evil good and good evil,[NOTE:1] who turn darkness into light and light into darkness,who turn bitter into sweet and sweet into bitter.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “Woe [to] those who call.” See the note at v. 8.
In this verse the prophet denounces the perversion of moral standards. Darkness and bitterness are metaphors for evil; light and sweetness symbolize uprightness.
verses.commentary:
5:20 "Woe to those who call evil good, and good evil" Many scholars say that this refers to the judges
of Israel. Although that fits Isa. 5:18-23, it seems to me that this is a reference to the society as a whole, not
limited to a group of judges. This is a poignant example of the tragedy of what happens when our light
becomes darkness (cf. Matt. 6:22-23). The fall of Genesis 3 has affected the moral compass of the creatures
made in the image and likeness (cf. Gen. 1:26-27) of the God of Justice, Righteousness, and Fairness!

This is the essence of the NT's "unpardonable sin."

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALLOF MANKIND

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE UNPARDONABLE SIN

verses.zh: 祸哉！那些自以为有智慧，自看为通达的人。
verses.en: Beware, those who think they are wise,[NOTE:1] those who think they possess understanding.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “the wise in their own eyes.”

Heb “[who] before their faces are understanding ones.”sn Verses 18-21 contain three “woe-sayings” that are purely accusatory and have no formal announcement of judgment attached (as in the “woe-sayings” recorded in vv. 8-17). While this lack of symmetry is odd, it has a clear rhetorical purpose. Having established a pattern in vv. 8-17, the prophet deviates from it in vv. 18-21 to grab his audience’s attention. By placing the “woes” in rapid succession and heaping up the accusatory elements, he highlights the people’s guilt and introduces an element of tension and anticipation. One is reasonably certain that judgment will come, and when it does, it will be devastating. This anticipated devastation is described in frightening detail after the sixth and final woe (see vv. 22-30).
verses.commentary:
5:21 "Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes,

And clever in their own sight" This again refers to the sin of prideful arrogance
(i.e. results of Genesis 3). Probably one of the most classical passages of this is Jer. 9:23-24 (also note Prov. 3:7; 1 Cor. 3:18-20).
Real wisdom is in knowing and trusting YHWH! Humans are smoke-blinded by self, sin, and their own
importance (cf. Prov. 26:5,12,16; 28:11).

verses.zh: 祸哉！那些勇于饮酒，以能力调浓酒的人。
verses.en: Beware, those who are champions[NOTE:1] at drinking, who display great courage when mixing strong drinks.
notes: The language used here is quite sarcastic and paves the way for the shocking description of the enemy army in vv. 25-30. The rich leaders of Judah are nothing but “party animals” who are totally incapable of withstanding real warriors.
verses.commentary:
5:22 "Woe to those who are heroes in drinking wine" Isaiah is using sarcasm because the term "heroes"
normally refers to "mighty men of war," but in this context it refers to "drinking bouts" and not military
exploits.

For "woe" see note at 1:8.

▣ "mixing strong drink" There has been some question as to what this (BDB 1016) refers.

- mixing wine with water, Isa. 1:22, like the Greeks and Romans, but the Isaiah texts refer to bad wine,
not normal drinking wine

- old strong wine mixed with new wine

- wine mixed with other distilled fruit or honey liquors, which made it more intoxicating (they did
not have fermented drinks with high alcohol content, as are available today)

This is the NOUN form of the VERB "to
become drunk." Drunkenness is condemned often in Scripture (cf. Isa. 5:11,22; 28:7; 56:12; Prov. 20:1;
23:29-35; Micah 2:11). It is even used as imagery for the judgment of YHWH (cf. Ps. 75:8).

SPECIAL TOPIC: BIBLICAL ATTITUDES TOWARD ALCOHOL AND ALCOHOLISM

verses.zh: 他们因受贿赂，就称恶人为义，将义人的义夺去。
verses.en: They pronounce the guilty innocent for a payoff,they ignore the just cause of the innocent.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “and the just cause of the innocent ones they turn aside from him.”sn In vv. 22-23 the prophet returns to themes with which he opened his speech. The accusatory elements of vv. 8, 11-12, 18-23 are arranged in a chiastic manner: (A) social injustice (8), (B) carousing (11-12a), (C) spiritual insensitivity (12b) // (C') spiritual insensitivity (18-21), (B') carousing (22), (A') social injustice (23).
verses.commentary:
5:23 "Who justify the wicked for a bribe" This is the place in the strophe where commentators discuss
the absence of a seventh woe. The interpretive question is whether there are seven woes (the perfect number)
or six woes (the number of human imperfection).

Bribery was regularly condemned in Isa. 1:23; 10:1-2 (cf. Exod. 23:8; Deut. 10:17; 16:19;
Prov. 17:23; Micah 3:11; 7:3).

▣ "the rights" This term (BDB 842) is a form of "righteousness." This is a crucial theological
term. YHWH chose it to describe His own character (i.e. Isa. 5:16) and fallen mankind's diviation from that standard.
See the important Special Topic below.

SPECIAL TOPIC: RIGHTEOUSNESS

verses.zh: 火苗怎样吞灭碎秸，干草怎样落在火焰之中，照样，他们的根必像朽物，他们的花必像灰尘飞腾；因为他们厌弃万军之耶和华的训诲，藐视以色列圣者的言语。
verses.en: Therefore, as flaming fire[NOTE:1] devours strawand dry grass disintegrates in the flames,so their root will rot,and their flower will blow away like dust.[NOTE:2] For they have rejected the law of the Lord of Heaven’s Armies,they have spurned the commands[NOTE:3] of the Holy One of Israel.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “a tongue of fire” (so NASB), referring to a tongue-shaped flame.
They are compared to a flowering plant that withers quickly in a hot, arid climate.
Heb “the word.”
See the note on the phrase “the Holy One of Israel” in 1:4.
verses.commentary:
5:24 Fire is imagery for judgment and cleansing (i.e., chaff and stubble burn quickly and
completely thereby not useful for cooking or heating, cf. Isa. 33:11; 47:14; Joel 2:5; Matt. 4:1).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FIRE

▣ "So their root will become like rot and their blossom blow away as dust" This is Hebrew
agricultural imagery for total destruction.

▣ "For they have rejected the law of the Lord of hosts,

And despised the word of the Holy One of Israel" This is the reason for judgment. It was
the willful, purposeful rejection of the Judean people of their covenant God (esp. Isa. 5:19). Notice
the two titles for Deity.

SPECIAL TOPIC: TERMS FOR GOD'S REVELATION

SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE HOLY ONE

verses.zh: 所以，耶和华的怒气向他的百姓发作。他的手伸出攻击他们，山岭就震动；他们的尸首在街市上好像粪土。虽然如此，他的怒气还未转消；他的手仍伸不缩。
verses.en: So the Lord is furious[NOTE:1] with his people;he lifts[NOTE:2] his hand and strikes them.The mountains shake,and corpses lie like manure[NOTE:3] in the middle of the streets.Despite all this, his anger does not subside,and his hand is ready to strike again.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “the anger of the Lord rages.”
Or “extends”; KJV, ASV “he hath stretched forth.”
Or “garbage” (NCV, CEV, NLT); NAB, NASB, NIV “refuse.”
Heb “in all this his anger is not turned, and still his hand is outstretched.”
verses.commentary:
5:25 "On this account the anger of the Lord has burned against His people"
Judgment will begin with the household of God. God's anger is as biblical a theme as is His love! The anger
is even accentuated in the presence of great light (cf. Luke 12:48).

SPECIAL TOPIC: GOD DESCRIBED AS HUMAN

▣ "And the mountains quaked" Many have assumed that this refers to the violent earthquake
recorded in the days of Uzziah (cf. Amos 1:1; Zech. 14:5). However, it may well be hyperbole of a Theophany.
Nature quakes at the coming of her Creator. This imagery is common in the OT (i.e., Isa. 64:3; Exod. 19:18;
Jer. 4:24; Joel 2:10; Nah. 1:5).

▣ "their corpses lay like refuse in the middle of the streets" OT people were shocked by unburied
bodies, rotting, exposed, or eaten by animals (i.e., Ezek. 39:4,17-20; Nahum 3:3). A proper burial affected
one's joy in the afterlife. It was a curse and horror to be unburied (cf. 1 Sam. 31:8-13).

SPECIAL TOPIC: BURIAL PRACTICES

▣ "His hand" See SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND

verses.zh: 他必竖立大旗，招远方的国民，发嘶声叫他们从地极而来；看哪，他们必急速奔来。
verses.en: He lifts a signal flag for a distant nation,[NOTE:1] he whistles for it to come from the far regions of the earth.Look, they[NOTE:2] come quickly and swiftly.
notes: The Hebrew text has literally, “for nations from a distance.” The following verses use singular forms to describe this nation, so the final mem (ם) on לְגּוֹיִם (legoyim) may be enclitic or dittographic. In the latter case one could read לְגוֹי מֵרָחוֹק (legoy merakhoq, “for a nation from a distance”; see Deut 28:49; Joel 3:8). Another possibility is to emend the text from לַגּוֹיִם מֵרָחוֹק (laggoyim merakhoq) to לְגוֹי מִמֶּרְחָק (legoy mimmerkhaq, “for a nation from a distant place”), a phrase which occurs in Jer 5:15. In this case an error of misdivision has occurred in MT, the mem of the prefixed preposition being accidentally taken as a plural ending on the preceding word.
Heb “he.” Singular forms are used throughout vv. 26-30 to describe this nation, but for stylistic reasons the translation uses the plural for these collective singulars.
verses.commentary:
5:26 "He will also lift up a standard to the distant nation" A "standard" or battle flag (BDB 651) was a way for
armies to communicate (cf. Isa. 11:12; 18:3; 30:17; 31:9; 49:22). It can be positive (restoration) or negative
(invasion) depending on the context. In this context it signals the invaders to come!

This is an extremely significant passage for the following reasons:

- notice that YHWH is in control of history, all history, as well as nature

- notice that YHWH lifts up a standard to the Gentile nations. Many have seen this verse as an allusion
to Deut. 28:49-57.

Within the book of Isaiah it seems to be a reference to the inclusion of the Gentiles
(cf. Isa. 2:2-4; 11:9,10,11; 27:13; 49:22; 56:7; 62:10; 66:19; see SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN)!

The term "nations" in the Masoretic text is PLURAL (LXX, Peshitta), goyim.
Most modern translations change it to SINGULAR, however, the PLURAL
possibly refers to an invading mercenary army made up of many nations. Assyria and Babylon conscripted
the soldiers of defeated armies into their ranks. The UBS Text Project, p. 13, gives the PLURAL
a "B" rating (some doubt).

▣ "will whistle for it" This is imagery for YHWH calling Gentile nations into conflict with His
own sinful people (cf. Isa. 7:18).

The same root (BDB 1056) also means "hiss" (BDB 1056, KB 1656, Qal
PERFECT with waw) as a sign of disgust, amazement, or derision. Here, it denotes a
signal for the nations to invade (cf. Isa. 7:18). This same imagery is positive in Zech. 10:8.

▣ "from the ends of the earth" This is a hyperbolic phrase. It denotes a nation out of the local
sphere of regular trade and politics. It reflects the covenant curse of Deut. 28:49.

verses.zh: 其中没有疲倦的，绊跌的；没有打盹的，睡觉的；腰带并不放松，鞋带也不折断。
verses.en: None tire or stumble,they don’t stop to nap or sleep.They don’t loosen their beltsor unstrap their sandals to rest.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “and the belt on his waist is not opened, and the thong of his sandals is not torn in two.”
verses.commentary:
5:27-30 This strophe describes the invincible invading army. They are not tired or weary. They do
not stumble because YHWH is with them! The shock of this description is that it follows the very terms
used to describe faithful Israel in Isa. 40:29-31. YHWH is against His own covenant people! He will
fight on behalf of the invading pagan enemy (cf. Habakkuk 1-2).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SECOND COMING, IV.

verses.zh: 他们的箭快利，弓也上了弦。马蹄算如坚石，车轮好像旋风。
verses.en: Their arrows are sharpened,and all their bows are prepared.[NOTE:1] The hooves of their horses are hard as flint,[NOTE:2] and their chariot wheels are like a windstorm.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “bent” (so KJV, NAB, NASB, NRSV); NIV “are strung.”
Heb “regarded like flint.”
They are like a windstorm in their swift movement and in the way they kick up dust.
verses.commentary:
5:28 "bows are bent" The Qal PASSIVE PARTICIPLE basically means
"to march" or "to tread upon." Here, it is used figuratively of how ancient archers fixed their bows for
action by stepping on them to get the string to cause the wooden shaft to bow (cf. Ps. 7:12; 11:2; Isa. 21:15;
Jer. 9:3; 46:9; 50:14). See Roland deVaux, Ancient Israel, p. 244.

▣ "like a whirlwind" The term (BDB 693) describes a destructive storm.

- literally, Isa. 17:13; 21:1; Job 21:18; 37:9; Ps. 83:15

- imagery, Isa. 29:6; Jer. 4:12-13

verses.en: At that time[NOTE:1] they will growl over their prey,[NOTE:2] it will sound like sea waves crashing against rocks.[NOTE:3] One will look out over the land and see the darkness of disaster,clouds will turn the light into darkness.[NOTE:4]
notes: Or “in that day” (KJV).
Heb “over it”; the referent (the prey) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “like the growling of the sea.”

The motif of light turning to darkness is ironic when compared to v. 20. There the sinners turn light (= moral/ethical good) to darkness (= moral/ethical evil). Now ironically the Lord will turn light (= the sinners’ sphere of existence and life) into darkness (= the judgment and death).tn Heb “and one will gaze toward the land, and look, darkness of distress, and light will grow dark by its [the land’s?] clouds.”

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for
your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority
in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject
divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the
original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

BACKGROUND STUDY

- It is difficult to know the historical context of this chapter. It may apply to any part of the
preaching ministry of Isaiah. Moderns do not know how the prophetic books were complied.
They are not chronological.

- Apparently this folk ballad was sung at some gathering of the nation of Judah. Whether it was in a
temple or in the marketplace is uncertain.

- It is important to remember that privilege brings responsibility (i.e., "the Two Ways," cf. Leviticus 26;
Deuteronomy 28; 30:15,19; Psalm 1; and note Luke 12:48).

- Allusions to the folk song are found in several places in the NT (cf. Matt. 21:33-46; Mark 12:1-2;
Luke 20:9-19).

- It must be remembered that Judah, during most of Isaiah's prophetic ministry (i.e., the eighth
century B.C.) was an extremely successful and prosperous nation. This
prosperity brought spiritual weakness and a dependency upon human resources instead of on
YHWH and His covenant promises and requirements.
